coverage: Nine stories · AI language energy, shopping agents, robot memory, bear alerts, lost telescope, DNA storage, life jackets, crowd quakes, NFL data

cards.headline: AI chatbots use more energy to answer in many non-English languages
cards.summary: University of Michigan researchers measured the energy three open-source AI models used across up to 122 languages. Non-English text took 1.4 to 180 times as much energy as English; Hindi needed 7.9 times and Bengali 15.3 times. The cause is tokens, the small text chunks a model processes: some languages split into many more tokens. Higher-energy languages also tended to get less accurate answers. The study was presented at the EMNLP 2026 conference.
cards.whyItMatters: Billions of people use AI in languages other than English. If those users pay more per token and get worse answers, the same tool is not equally fair or useful for everyone.

csp.connection: Design choices, such as how text is split into tokens, can create unequal costs and quality for different groups of users.

cards.headline: Study finds AI shopping helpers pushed pricier picks to wealthier users
cards.summary: Researchers from Carnegie Mellon and Cisco ran about 325,000 tests of 13 AI models acting as personal agents, programs that pick flights, insurance or graduate schools for a user. Given identical requests from 32 fictional people, 8 of the 13 models chose more expensive options for wealthier profiles, sometimes guessing wealth from a single email. Only hiding financial details largely closed the gap. The study is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and used fictional users.
cards.whyItMatters: AI helpers are being given access to email and personal data. What an agent knows about you can change its choices, so privacy settings affect more than who sees your data.

csp.connection: Personal data used as an algorithm's input can change its output in ways users did not request or expect.

cards.headline: MIT robots learn to double-check what they remember seeing
cards.summary: Robots that label objects with AI can mistake a chimney for a squirrel and keep that wrong memory. MIT researchers built a system that scores how uncertain each label is by checking the AI's confidence and comparing views from different angles. When a label looks shaky, it picks a few more images to re-check. It resolved ambiguity for about 92% of objects using two extra captions each. The work is an arXiv preprint headed to the NeurIPS conference.
cards.whyItMatters: Robots in homes, hospitals and warehouses need to know when they might be wrong. Checking evidence from several angles is also a good habit for people judging information.

csp.connection: Comparing several independent inputs and measuring agreement lets an algorithm detect and correct its own likely errors.

cards.headline: Engineer builds crowdsourced bear-warning website in Kashmir
cards.summary: Mudasir Ali, a software engineer in Kashmir, built Wildping after his mother died in a bear attack. On the free website, people report sightings of Himalayan black bears and leopards, and users who set "watch zones" around homes, farms or school paths get phone alerts when an animal is reported nearby. It had about 9,000 visitors in under a month. It has not been shown to reduce attacks; its own site says it can buy families a few minutes.
cards.whyItMatters: A single programmer turned a personal loss into a tool for a whole region. Apps built on community reports work only when enough people take part.

csp.connection: Crowdsourcing collects data from many users; its usefulness depends on how many people contribute and how accurate their reports are.

cards.headline: NASA's Swift telescope burns up after robot rescue falls short
cards.summary: NASA's Swift observatory studied cosmic explosions for two decades, but atmospheric drag pulled it lower. A robotic spacecraft called LINK, built by the company Katalyst Space, launched in July to grab Swift and boost its orbit. LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels, which help a spacecraft control its orientation, and began spinning. Engineers uploaded new control software, but the capture was called off. Swift reentered over Indonesia on November 4.
cards.whyItMatters: Satellites depend on software and backup systems to recover from failures. Engineers say future repair missions need spare fuel and fault-tolerant designs, not just enough power to reach a target.

csp.connection: Fault tolerance means designing systems with redundancy so they can keep working when some parts fail.

cards.headline: Automated microfactory stores digital files in DNA
cards.summary: A European team tested DNAMIC, an automated system that writes digital files into synthetic DNA. It translates binary 0s and 1s into DNA's four chemical letters, A, T, G and C, a process that can take several hours. The team stored a Swiss watchmaking archive and sealed the DNA in small steel capsules that need no power to preserve it. The University of Geneva announced the test; claims that the DNA lasts tens of thousands of years are projections.
cards.whyItMatters: The world produces enormous amounts of data, and today's hard drives need power and replacing. DNA could hold archives far more compactly, but writing and reading it is still slow.

csp.connection: Any data can be stored in any medium with enough distinct symbols; binary can be re-encoded into DNA's four-letter code.

cards.headline: Battery-free device turns wave motion into a life jacket SOS light
cards.summary: Australia's University of Wollongong researchers built a soft device with two liquid-metal droplets in a conductive liquid. Movement shifts the droplets, producing a small current. Forty linked devices made about 2 volts, enough to light small LEDs, and a life-jacket prototype used wave motion to light an "SOS" sign. It can also sense bending and even a wrist pulse. Researchers say power and durability need improvement. The study is in Science Advances.
cards.whyItMatters: Many sensors and wearables stop working when batteries die. Devices that power themselves from movement could work in places where charging is impractical.

csp.connection: Sensors convert physical events, like motion or pressure, into electrical signals a computing system can read.

cards.headline: Earthquake sensors can tell marching crowds from casual walkers
cards.summary: A Tel Aviv University seismologist analyzed ground-shaking data recorded during a 2020 march of about 11,000 people in New York state and a 2021 pilgrimage of about 100,000 in Israel. Tokyo schoolyard sensors also picked up school activity. Coordinated crowds that march, jump or chant created stronger signals than similar-sized casual crowds, mostly at 1 to 2 vibrations per second, close to walking pace. The study is in Seismological Research Letters.
cards.whyItMatters: Sensors built for one purpose can reveal unexpected patterns in other data. The author hopes to learn whether signals could someday reveal changes in crowd behavior, which is not yet shown.

csp.connection: Analyzing patterns in large sensor datasets can reveal information that the data was never originally collected to show.

cards.headline: Carnegie Mellon trains AI on NFL game film and tracking data
cards.summary: The NFL gave Carnegie Mellon University researchers official game film and Next Gen Stats data, which come from chips in players' shoulder pads, equipment and the ball that record movement on the field. The team received several terabytes and built two starting AI models: one learns from video and one from tracking data. Goals include automatically labeling plays and predicting moves like blitzes. The project is early, and no accuracy results have been reported yet.
cards.whyItMatters: Coaches and scouts spend many hours labeling game film by hand. Sports analytics is a growing career path that combines statistics, programming and a love of the game.

csp.connection: Combining different types of data, such as video and location tracking, can reveal patterns that neither shows alone.
